title: Check yourself: reading the MTI and the bitmaps

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Your issuer host answered a reversal advice, 0420, an hour ago. The same advice now arrives again as 0421, because the acquirer never saw your answer. Which MTI does your new answer carry?

options.text: 0430, since the answer is the same whether the advice came once or twice
options.says: 2.1: a repeat is answered like the original, so 0420 and its repeat 0421 both get 0430

options.text: 0431, since the answer has to show which copy of the advice it is for
options.says: 2.1: both the 0420 and its repeat get 0430; the answer carries no repeat mark

options.text: 0421 sent back, since a repeated advice is acknowledged by returning it
options.says: 2.1: an advice gets an advice response, third digit 3; nothing is acknowledged by echoing the request MTI

options.text: 0410 sent back, since a reversal is answered as a request response
options.says: 2.1: the third digit of 0421 is 2, an advice, so its response is 3 (0430), not 1

origin.section: 2.1. The MTI's Four Digits Say Edition, Class, Function and Origin

questions.stem: A new sender's messages unpack without errors on your host, yet the amounts in your log don't match the merchants' receipts. For the same fields, each bit in its bitmaps sits one place to the right of where your own messages put it. What does that say about the fields your host read from those messages?

options.text: Every field holds another field's data, since each was cut out with a length meant for a different field
options.says: 2.2.1: the receiver trusts the bitmap and reads each field with the definition of the next one; the shifted purchase with field 37 unpacked with field 4 = 111111111111

options.text: Every field holds its own data, since a message that unpacks cleanly had a bitmap the host accepted
options.says: 2.2.1: the shifted purchase with field 37 unpacked without an error and with wrong values, so a clean unpack can hide a shifted bitmap

options.text: Only the amount is misread, since the fixed-length fields after the moved bits realign the rest
options.says: 2.2.1: nothing realigns; field 3 took the length prefix and the card number's first digits, and every later field started in the wrong place

options.text: Only the amount is misread, since the receiver checks the other fields against their definitions
options.says: 2.2.1: the digits of a card number were accepted as a processing code and as an amount

origin.section: 2.2.1. Spot the Problem: The Vendor's First Purchase

questions.stem: Two messages go out on an iso87ascii link. The first carries fields 3, 4, 11, 41 and a MAC in field 64, and its bitmap part is 16 characters; the second carries fields 3, 4, 11, 41 and field 90, and its bitmap part is 32. Why the difference?

options.text: Field 64 is announced by the primary bitmap's last bit, and field 90 needs a second bitmap
options.says: 2.2 and 2.3: bit 64 is the primary bitmap's last bit, so field 64 fits one bitmap; field 90 needs the secondary one, announced by bit 1

options.text: Field 64 is left out of the bitmap as a MAC, and field 90 needs a second bitmap
options.says: 2.2 and 2.3: field 64 is a field like any other, announced by bit 64 of the primary bitmap

options.text: Field 90 belongs to reversals, and reversal fields always bring a second bitmap
options.says: 2.3: the second bitmap follows from the field number, any field from 65 to 128; the echo test in 2.3 needs one for field 70

options.text: Field 90 is longer than field 64, and long fields always bring a second bitmap
options.says: 2.3: the bitmap says which fields are present, not how long they are; field 90 needs the secondary bitmap because its number is above 64

origin.section: 2.3. Bit 1 Announces a Second Bitmap, So It Is Never a Field

questions.stem: On a new link, your iso87ascii packager fails on the host's first message with an index or length error. The host's specification describes the bitmap as b 64. What do you check first?

options.text: The captured bitmap's size, since links differ: some send b 64 as raw bytes, others as hex digits
options.says: 2.4: the same 64 bits travel in either form, the bytes don't say which, and each link's specification decides

options.text: The captured bitmap's size, since links differ: some send b 64 as 64 characters, others as 64 bytes
options.says: 2.4: 64 is the number of bits, which travel as 8 bytes or as 16 hexadecimal characters

options.text: The field lengths, since packagers agree: every 1987 packager writes b 64 the same way
options.says: 2.4: iso87ascii and iso87binary are both 1987 packagers and write the bitmap as 16 characters and as 8 bytes

options.text: The field lengths, since errors agree: an index error comes from a field, not from a bitmap
options.says: 2.4: iso87ascii failed on the binary message's bitmap with an index error, before reading any data field

origin.section: 2.4. The Same Bits Travel as 8 Bytes or as 16 Characters

concepts: The same 64 bits travel as 8 bytes or 16 hexadecimal characters, as each link's specification says, and the bytes don't tell which.
A message whose highest field is 64 has one bitmap; any field above 64 brings the secondary bitmap.
A response changes the MTI's third digit and a repeat its fourth, and a repeat is answered like the original.
A receiver trusts the bitmap, so a bitmap off by one bit reads every field with another field's definition and may still unpack.
